prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The speaker reflects on bodily anxiety, remorse, and ecological devastation by linking a quivering heart to Earth’s self-destructive natural wealth through visceral imagery and cosmic perspective. Despite distrust, shame, and anticipated loss, the speaker remains bound to Earth as intimately as blood, revealing how grief and attachment persist amid planetary ruin.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Just, And, This

outputs.L1:
Just now, I touched my chest and felt my heart quivering there. This must be one of the bad times. I think it is quivering with remorse and exhaustion.

Once, in a documentary, I saw a heart beating. I was a very little girl, and the sight disgusted me. Throbbing without cease, my heart betrays me and yet remains sure and true—a thing of nature.

The Earth, bleeding its guts out onto the seafloor, exhausts me with remorse and shame; and yet I have to trust it, as wealth is proven by how terribly it devastates itself, and I am but one symptom among billions of the wealth of Earth.

A tired feeling, recuperated by a passing spaceship or an infinitude like fame, but more universal.

I will have to miss you, Earth; I miss you already. And yet, when I touch myself—whom I should not trust—it is still only the heaviest and most jealous feelings that bind me to you, like blood.
outputs.L2:
A moment ago, I pressed a hand against my chest  
and sensed my heart trembling beneath it.  
This must be one of the difficult periods.  
Perhaps regret and weariness are making it shake.  

When I was very young, I watched a documentary  
that showed a living heart at work,  
and the image repelled me.  

Now my own heart pulses without pause.  
It exposes me, yet stays faithful and steady—  
an unquestionable piece of the natural world.  

The Earth spills its insides across the ocean floor,  
filling me with fatigue, guilt, and disgrace.  
Still, I must place my faith in it,  
because its abundance is demonstrated  
through the dreadful violence it inflicts upon itself.  
I am only one of billions of signs  
of the planet’s richness.  

This exhaustion is briefly restored  
by a spacecraft moving past,  
or by something boundless—resembling fame,  
but belonging to the whole universe.  

Earth, I will be forced to long for you;  
I am longing for you even now.  
And when I lay a hand on the self  
I know I should distrust,  
I find that only my most burdensome, possessive emotions  
fasten me to you,  
as intimately as blood.
outputs.L3:
During a moment of profound difficulty, the speaker becomes acutely aware of their heart quivering with remorse and exhaustion. Its persistent beating once inspired disgust, perhaps because it seemed too physical, vulnerable, or indifferent to suffering. Yet the speaker now recognizes the heart as something steady and trustworthy—a natural force that continues its work even when thought, hope, and certainty begin to fail.

This personal turmoil reflects a larger crisis. Earth’s destructive, self-devastating processes fill the speaker with shame, remorse, and weariness. They do not view themselves as separate from this damage, but as one of billions of symptoms produced by the planet’s troubled abundance: a single life among countless others, all implicated in the excess, conflict, and suffering of the world.

Even so, alienation does not sever the speaker’s connection to Earth. Mistrust persists, and separation may be unavoidable, whether through estrangement or death. Nevertheless, the bond remains intense and bodily. The speaker is tied to the planet by feelings as deep and vital as blood—a connection that endures despite disgust, guilt, fatigue, and fear.
outputs.L4:
The speaker begins with the body, describing anxiety as a physical disturbance: the heart trembles, blood pulses uneasily, and remorse seems to inhabit the flesh. This private agitation gradually expands into an image of the planet itself. Earth’s forests, minerals, waters, and other forms of natural abundance become a destructive wealth—resources that invite exploitation and allow humanity to consume the very world on which it depends. Through visceral imagery, the speaker makes environmental devastation feel like an injury within the body, while a cosmic perspective reveals the scale and fragility of Earth’s suffering.

The speaker’s relationship with the planet is therefore marked by contradiction. Distrust and shame arise from witnessing, and perhaps participating in, the systems that damage the natural world. The speaker also anticipates loss, recognizing that familiar landscapes, species, and forms of life may disappear. Yet this knowledge does not produce detachment. Instead, grief intensifies the bond: Earth remains as intimate and indispensable as blood, circulating through the speaker’s identity and existence. Even amid planetary ruin, attachment persists, suggesting that love for the world can survive alongside guilt, fear, and despair.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in which the speaker touches their chest, feels their heart quiver, and connects bodily unease with guilt over humanity’s devastation of Earth.
counterfactuals.output:
I press my palm against my chest  
as if to quiet a door  
someone is trying to open from within.

My heart quivers—  
small animal beneath the ribs,  
startled by its own shelter.

Perhaps it has heard the forests falling,  
each trunk a bone giving way.  
Perhaps it has swallowed  
the warm, oil-dark sea,  
the gull’s plastic hunger,  
the last thin cry  
of ice departing from ice.

I breathe,  
but the air arrives carrying smoke  
from fires I did not light  
and fed with every ordinary wanting.

What innocence can the body claim  
when the hands have taken,  
the mouth consumed,  
the feet crossed a wounded world  
and called the road progress?

Still, the heart trembles—  
not absolution,  
not yet grief enough—

only this fragile knocking,  
asking whether guilt  
can become a kind of mercy,

whether the hand on my chest  
might learn to reach outward,  
to touch the ruined earth  
without taking more.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental prose poem about remorse, exhaustion, ecological collapse, and the conflicted intimacy between the human body and the planet. Include memories of seeing a beating heart in a documentary and imagery of a passing spaceship.
counterfactuals.output:
I remember the documentary: a heart lifted into light,  
still beating as if the body were a rumor  
it refused to believe.

Red muscle. Small, tireless animal.  
The camera did not look away.  
I did.

Years later, remorse has learned that rhythm—  
its wet fist opening, closing,  
opening again around what cannot be repaired.

Outside, the forests practice becoming smoke.  
The sea coughs plastic onto the shore.  
Each glacier withdraws its white hand  
from ours.

I am so tired I mistake exhaustion for innocence.  
I sleep beneath the fan’s mechanical weather,  
my breath borrowing oxygen from trees  
I have never thanked,  
my blood carrying the salt of an ancient ocean  
we are warming past recognition.

What intimacy is this:  
to be made of the wounded thing,  
to hunger through it,  
to press my heel into the soil  
and call the pressure love?

At dusk a spaceship passes overhead—  
not a star, not salvation,  
only a bright rivet moving through the dark.  
For one moment I imagine it looking down:

the continents lit like failing organs,  
storms turning in their beds,  
cities burning their necklaces of fuel.

Inside me, that remembered heart  
keeps beating without permission.

Inside the earth, buried heat.  
Inside the heat, our engines.  
Inside our engines, the old desire  
to leave no limit unbroken.

I place my palm against my chest,  
then against the ground.

Between them:  
a thin wall,  
a terrible resemblance,

and the pulse continuing—  
not forgiveness,  
not yet—

but something exhausted  
trying, impossibly,  
to remain alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, melancholic poem from the perspective of someone already mourning Earth, blending visceral images of blood and organs with reflections on wealth, environmental destruction, fame, and cosmic distance.
counterfactuals.output:
**Elegy Sent Before the Planet Dies**

I began mourning Earth while she was still warm,  
while her blue lung opened beneath the clouds  
and the forests—those dark, elaborate organs—  
kept lifting their green hands to the sun.

Already I could hear the saws  
circling the century like flies.  
Rivers dragged their silver intestines  
through cities jeweled with oil.  
At dusk, the refineries blossomed—  
black roses fed by buried blood.

We called it wealth:  
the locked room, the polished bone,  
the numbers breeding behind glass.  
Men with clean cuffs purchased mountains  
and wore them down to gravel.  
Women sold their faces to the satellites,  
and fame passed over us  
like a fever with perfect teeth.

I, too, wanted to be seen.  
I pressed my name into the wound of the world  
and waited for applause.  
Somewhere, a glacier calved  
with the sound of a cathedral  
remembering it had a body.

Earth, forgive us—  
we mistook your marrow for merchandise,  
your coral hearts for ornaments,  
your whales for vaults of meat and song.  
We dipped our hands into your opened chest  
and counted the coins that came out red.

Now every screen is a small moon  
showing us ourselves:  
bright, distant, already dead.  
Celebrities shine in their rented heavens,  
their grief sponsored, their tears  
tiny diamonds no ocean can afford.

At night I look beyond the atmosphere,  
past Mars with its rusted mouth,  
past the cold machinery of stars.  
Light travels years to touch my face,  
bringing news of fires long extinguished.

Perhaps somewhere, impossibly far,  
another creature looks toward us  
and sees only a pale blue ghost—  
not the smokestacks, not the plastic tide,  
not the last bird falling  
through an avenue of cameras,

but Earth as she was:  
a wet heart turning in the dark,  
alone among the distances,  
her veins full of thunder,  
her fragile ribs crowded  
with those who loved her too late.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-stanza contemporary poem that begins with heart palpitations and expands into an existential meditation on nature, shame, exploitation, and humanity as one symptom among billions.
counterfactuals.output: Heart palpitations—small fists knocking from inside the rented room of my body, while outside, the trees keep their green counsel and the river drags a silver bruise through town; I think of shame, how it clings like oil to the hands that profit, how every bright package carries a hidden forest, every convenience its exhausted animal, every screen a mine collapsing in someone else’s night. The wind turns the leaves without asking who owns them. Fungi translate the dead into another language of hunger. Beneath our roads, roots touch in the dark, exchanging warnings we have priced beyond hearing. Perhaps humanity is not the fever but one symptom among billions: a brief red flare in the blood of the planet, no more singular than plankton, plague, grief, or rain. Still, my heart keeps misfiring its little emergency, insisting I am here, I am afraid, as if existence were a door only panic could open, as if the earth, exploited and patient, had placed its trembling in my chest.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an intimate eco-poem in a fragmented, stream-of-consciousness style. Compare the speaker’s mistrusted but faithful heart to an Earth that “bleeds its guts out” while devastating itself, and end with blood as the bond between them.
counterfactuals.output:
you never trusted my heart—  
that small red animal  
under the ribs,  
startled by every tenderness  
yet returning, returning  

like rain to a poisoned field.

I think of Earth at night,  
turning in her fever,  
forests lit like torn letters,  
rivers swallowing plastic prayers,  
her bright machines biting deeper  
because hunger forgets its own mouth—

she bleeds its guts out  
while devastating itself,  
mother and wound,  
knife and flesh,  
still cradling seeds  
in the ash.

and my heart, mistrusted thing,  
does the same:  
ruins its rooms,  
floods them,  
then waits in the doorway  
faithful as moss,  
holding your name  
where the light gets in.

listen—  
beneath us, within me,  
the same wet vow:

blood,  
the bond between us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
